claims.text: HfNbTiVAl10 has a well-defined hierarchical heterostructure comprising nanoscale clusters and interfacing phases.
Combining mesoscale heterostructure simulations with machine learning will enable rapid prediction of mechanical properties in HfNbTiVAl10.
The hybrid model will predict Young's modulus under tensile testing.
The hybrid model will predict yield strength under tensile testing.
The hybrid model will predict fracture-related behavior under fracture testing.
The hybrid model will be at least 10% more accurate than established full-scale simulations.
The hybrid model will require up to 50% less computational time than established full-scale simulations.
A hierarchical heterostructure channels heterogeneous phase and interface behavior into macroscopic mechanical responses.
Phase distribution, nanoscale clustering, and interface integrity govern key deformation and failure mechanisms.
Focusing simulations on dominant microstructural features reduces simulation complexity.
Reducing simulation complexity by focusing on dominant microstructural features produces faster and more accurate predictions.
Predictions will deviate by no more than 10% from experimental measurements.
Conventional full-scale molecular-dynamics or finite-element simulations require greater computational resources and longer runtimes to achieve similar accuracy.
The approach may fail when hierarchical features are insufficiently resolved.
High temperatures may induce phase transformations that cause prediction failure when those transformations are absent from the training data.
Large deviations in microstructural uniformity may impair the model's ability to generalize.
Predictive-accuracy and efficiency gains may vary with alloy batch and testing conditions.

contradictions.description: The accuracy target changes between a relative improvement of at least 10% over conventional simulations and an absolute prediction error of no more than 10%; these are not equivalent criteria.
The runtime claim is stated as 'up to 50% less,' which permits reductions below 50%, but the predicted outcome and falsification rule require approximately a 50% reduction.

The parenthetical explanation equates failure to achieve a 10% accuracy improvement with having error equal to or greater than the conventional model's error, omitting cases with a positive but less-than-10% improvement.
